content.title: About
content.content: Amaranth groats are the tiny seeds of amaranth (Amaranthus), native to the Americas. Amaranth is a pseudocereal, meaning its seeds are used like a grain, but the plant is not a cereal. The groats have a nutty, earthy, slightly grassy flavor. When cooked, they become sticky with a fine crunchy texture. Amaranth is cooked as porridge, added to baked goods and soups, and popped like popcorn.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Amaranth is a pseudocereal, not a true cereal.
The Aztecs grew amaranth and used it in rituals; according to tradition, Spanish conquerors banned its cultivation.
Amaranth leaves are also edible and resemble spinach.
Amaranth seeds can be popped in a dry hot pot like popcorn; in Mexico they are made into a sweet called alegría.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Amaranth protein has a good amino acid profile, including lysine.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and helps you feel full.

items.title: Contains magnesium and manganese
items.content: These minerals support metabolism and muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Contains iron and calcium
items.content: These minerals support oxygen transport and bone health.

items.title: Suitable for gluten-free diets
items.content: Pure amaranth can be part of a gluten-free diet when properly labeled.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Amaranth contains oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit.

items.title: Antinutrients
items.content: Phytates can reduce mineral absorption; cooking and soaking reduce them.

items.title: Bloating
items.content: A sudden increase in fiber intake can cause bloating.

items.title: Gluten contamination
items.content: People with celiac disease should choose groats labeled gluten-free because of possible cross-contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rinse the groats in a fine sieve and cook them in water in a ratio of about 1 to 2–3 for about 20 minutes until soft; the texture turns sticky. Use them in porridge, soups, patties, and baked goods. For puffed amaranth, toast the seeds in small batches in a dry hot pot.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store groats in an airtight container in a dry, cool, dark place; for long storage, the refrigerator is better, since the oils can turn rancid. Keep cooked groats in the refrigerator for three to five days.

bacon-lettuce-tomato-sandwich-on-wheat.title: Bacon, Lettuce, Tomato Sandwich on Wheat

content.title: About
content.content: The bacon, lettuce, and tomato sandwich on wheat is a classic American BLT, made with crispy bacon, fresh lettuce leaves, juicy tomato slices, and whole‑wheat bread. It balances salty, fresh, and slightly sweet flavors, providing a mix of protein, vegetables, and carbohydrates.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sandwich is commonly called a “BLT,” using the first letters of its main ingredients.
The first printed BLT recipe appeared in the United States in the early 1920s, but it gained widespread popularity after World War II.
Traditional BLT bread is lightly toasted to prevent sogginess from the sauce.
Variations may include mayo, avocado, cheese, or swapping bacon for turkey for a lighter version.
The combination of bacon and tomato is said to enhance the perception of umami flavor.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Bacon provides high‑quality animal protein, essential for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Lettuce supplies vitamin K, important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Lycopene in tomatoes
items.content: Tomatoes are high in lycopene, an antioxidant linked to heart health and reduced risk of certain cancers.

items.title: Whole‑wheat bread
items.content: Whole‑wheat bread adds dietary fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals that support digestion.

items.title: Energy balance
items.content: The mix of protein, fat, and carbs provides a quick and sustained energy boost.

items.title: High sodium and saturated fat
items.content: Bacon is high in salt and saturated fats, which can raise blood pressure and cardiovascular risk if eaten frequently.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat bread contains gluten, which may cause reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The sandwich is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Nitrites in bacon
items.content: Some bacon is cured with nitrites, which can form potentially harmful compounds when overcooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Typically the bread is lightly toasted, spread with mayo or mustard, then layered with lettuce, tomato slices, crispy bacon, and topped with the second slice of bread. It can be eaten by hand or cut in half for a neater bite.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared sandwich in the refrigerator, wrapped in plastic film or in an airtight container, for up to 24 hours. Keep bacon separate from the vegetables to avoid soggy bread. For longer storage, keep ingredients separate and assemble the sandwich just before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Bread, rice, toasted is a ready‑to‑eat product consisting of bread slices infused with cooked rice and lightly toasted to a golden crust. It combines the softness of rice with the crisp texture of bread, making it a convenient snack or side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bread‑and‑rice combination is traditional in Asian cuisine as a quick source of energy.
Toasting creates a characteristic aroma and enhances flavor through the Maillard reaction.
The product is often packaged in single‑serve portions, ideal for travel and outdoor activities.
Rice adds extra carbohydrates, while bread provides fiber and a modest amount of protein.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Carbohydrates from both rice and bread quickly replenish glycogen stores, beneficial during physical activity.

items.title: Convenient consumption
items.content: The product is ready to eat without further preparation, saving time.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Bread, especially whole‑grain varieties, contains B1, B2, and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: Bread contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: The combination of bread and rice can raise blood sugar quickly, which should be considered by individuals with diabetes.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Some versions may contain added salt; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy it as a standalone snack, add to salads, use as a base for sandwiches, or serve alongside soups. For a softer texture, you may briefly warm it in the microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed package. For extended storage, keep refrigerated to prevent drying out and spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned pear in a juice pack (item 4019) consists of whole pieces of ripe pear sealed in a hermetic pouch with its own juice. The product retains the fruit's natural taste, aroma, and nutrients, while being convenient for transport and storage.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pears belong to the Rosaceae family and are close relatives of apples and plums.
Juice‑pack canning preserves up to 80 % of vitamin C, which is often lost during traditional heat processing.
The juice in the pack is frequently used as a natural sweetener in cooking.
Pears are rich in dietary fiber, which supports digestive health.
A small amount of citric acid is usually added to stabilize colour and flavour.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy bowel function, increases satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in maintaining normal blood pressure and heart function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Canned pears contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols in pears help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Pear allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pears, ranging from skin rashes to severe symptoms.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Canned pears contain added sugars, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Preservative additives
items.content: Certain batches may contain preservatives (e.g., potassium sorbate); check the label if you are sensitive.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pear juice packs can be eaten straight from the pouch, added to salads, desserts, yogurts, cereals, or used in baking. They also work well in sauces and marinades.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened pouch in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days.
